n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you must not go into them, and they must not go into you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Surely they will bend your heart after their gods.” The words “if you do” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Solomon clung to them for love.” The pronominal suffix, translated “them,” is masculine here, even though it appears the foreign women are in view. Perhaps this is due to attraction to the masculine forms used of the nations earlier in the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wives, princesses.”

*Study note:* *Concubines* were slave women in ancient Near Eastern societies who were the legal property of their master, but who could have legitimate sexual relations with their master. A concubine’s status was more elevated than a mere servant, but she was not free and did not have the legal rights of a free wife. The children of a concubine could, in some instances, become equal heirs with the children of the free wife. The usage in the present passage suggests that after the period of the Judges concubines may have become more of a royal prerogative (cf. also {{2 Samuel 21:10|2 Sam 21:10-14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his wives bent his heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bent his heart after.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his heart was not complete with the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walked after.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Milcom, the detestable thing of the Ammonites.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* The idiomatic statement reads in Hebrew, “he did not fill up after.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “then.”

*Study note:* *The hill east of Jerusalem* refers to the Mount of Olives.

*Study note:* *A high place*. The “high places” were places of worship that were naturally or artificially elevated (see {{1 Kings 3:2|1 Kgs 3:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Chemosh, the detestable thing of Moab.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “Molech,” but Milcom must be intended (see vv. {{1 Kings 11:5|5}}, {{1 Kings 11:33|33}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the same thing he did for all his foreign wives, [who] were burning incense and sacrificing to their gods.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bent his heart.”

*Study note:* These *two occasions* are mentioned in {{1 Kings 3:5|1 Kgs 3:5}} and {{1 Kings 9:2|9:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and had commanded him concerning this thing not to walk after other gods.”

*Translator's note:* Or “keep.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Because this is with you, and you have not kept my covenant and my rules which I commanded you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until he had cut off every male in Edom.”

*Translator's note:* The MT reads “Adad,” an alternate form of the name Hadad.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Adad fled, he and Edomite men from the servants of his father, to go to Egypt, and Hadad was a small boy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they arose from Midian and went to Paran and they took men with them from Paran and went to Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt and he gave to him a house and food he said to him, and a land he gave to him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Hadad found great favor in the eyes of Pharaoh.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he gave to him a wife, the sister of his wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bore him Genubath his son.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads וַתִּגְמְלֵהוּ (vattigmelehu, “weaned him”) but a slight alteration of the consonantal text yields וַתִּגְדְלֵהוּ (vattigdelehu, “raised him”), which seems to make better sense.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down with his fathers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “send me away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Indeed what do you lack with me, that now you are seeking to go to your land?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said.”

*Study note:* *So Hadad asked Pharaoh*…. This lengthy description of Hadad’s exile in Egypt explains why Hadad wanted to oppose Solomon and supports the author’s thesis that his hostility to Solomon found its ultimate source in divine providence. Though Hadad enjoyed a comfortable life in Egypt, when the Lord raised him up (apparently stirring up his desire for vengeance) he decided to leave the comforts of Egypt and return to Edom.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (Solomon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he was the officer of a raiding band.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads “when David killed them.” This phrase is traditionally joined with what precedes. The ancient Greek version does not reflect the phrase and some suggest that it has been misplaced from the end of v. {{1 Kings 11:23|23}}.
*Translator's note:* The construction (Qal of קוּץ + בְּ [quts + bet] preposition) is rare, but not without parallel (see Lev 20:23).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “raised a hand against.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Ephrathite,” which here refers to an Ephraimite (see *HALOT* 81 s.v. אֶפְרַיִם).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this is the matter concerning which he raised a hand against the king.”

*Study note:* *The city of his father David*. The phrase refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See {{2 Samuel 5:7|2 Sam 5:7}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has simply “he,” making it a bit unclear whether Jeroboam or Ahijah is the subject, but in the Hebrew word order Ahijah is the nearer antecedent, and this is followed by the present translation.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Ahijah grabbed the new robe that was on him.”

*Translator's note:* The words “I am taking the kingdom from him” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Text-critical note:* This is the reading of the MT; the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “he has.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walked in my ways.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by doing what is right in my eyes, my rules and my regulations, like David his father.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I will give it to you, 10 tribes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “give.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so there might be a lamp for David my servant all the days before me in Jerusalem.” The metaphorical “lamp” symbolizes the Davidic dynasty. Because this imagery is unfamiliar to the modern reader, the translation “so my servant David’s dynasty may continue to serve me” has been used.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so there might be a lamp for David my servant all the days before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen for myself to put my name there.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “If you obey.” In the Hebrew text v. {{1 Kings 11:38|38}} is actually one long conditional sentence, which has been broken into two parts in the translation for stylistic purposes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walk in my ways.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do what is right in my eyes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will build for you a permanent house, like I built for David.”

*Study note:* *Because of this*. Reference is made to the idolatry mentioned earlier.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but not all the days.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but Jeroboam arose and ran away to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the events of Solomon, and all which he did, and his wisdom, are they not written on the scroll of the events of Solomon?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down with his fathers.”

*Study note:* *The city of his father David*. The phrase refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See {{2 Samuel 5:7|2 Sam 5:7}}.

*Text-critical note:* Before this sentence the Old Greek translation includes the following words: “And it so happened that when Jeroboam son of Nebat heard—now he was in Egypt where he had fled from before Solomon and was residing in Egypt—he came straight to his city in the land of Sarira which is on mount Ephraim. And king Solomon slept with his fathers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “come [to].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* Verse {{1 Kings 12:2|2}} is not included in the Old Greek translation. See the note on {{1 Kings 11:43|11:43}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jeroboam lived in Egypt.” The parallel text in 2 Chr 10:2 reads, “and Jeroboam returned from Egypt.” In a purely consonantal text the forms “and he lived” and “and he returned” are identical (וישׁב).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “They sent and called for him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “made our yoke burdensome.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but you, now, lighten the burdensome work of your father and the heavy yoke which he placed on us, and we will serve you.” In the Hebrew text the prefixed verbal form with vav (וְנַעַבְדֶךָ, [venaʿavdekha] “and we will serve you”) following the imperative (הָקֵל [haqel], “lighten”) indicates purpose (or result). The conditional sentence used in the translation above is an attempt to bring out the logical relationship between these forms.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and serve them and answer them,” understood as “serve them in how you answer them,” hence “grant their request.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and speak to them good words.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the days.” The Hebrew phrase contrasts what he is asked to do “today” (literally “the day”) with the benefit for “all the days.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “He rejected the advice of the elders which they advised and he consulted the young men with whom he had grown up, who stood before him.” The referent (Rehoboam) of the initial pronoun (“he”) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* In the Hebrew text the verb “we will respond” is plural, although it can be understood as an editorial “we.” The ancient versions have the singular here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Lighten the yoke which your father placed on us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter upon us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My little one is thicker than my father’s hips.” The referent of “my little one” is not clear. The traditional view is that it refers to the little finger. As the following statement makes clear, Rehoboam’s point is that he is more harsh and demanding than his father.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and now my father placed upon you a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” “Scorpions” might allude to some type of torture using poisonous insects, but more likely it refers to a type of whip that inflicts an especially biting, painful wound. Cf. CEV “whips with pieces of sharp metal.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and spoke to them according to.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” See the note on the same phrase in v. {{1 Kings 12:11|11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because this turn of events was from the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that he might bring to pass his word which the Lord spoke.”

*Study note:* *We have no portion in David; no share in the son of Jesse*. Their point seems to be that they have no familial relationship with David that brings them any benefits or places upon them any obligations. They are being treated like outsiders.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to your tents, Israel.” The word “return” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Now see your house, David.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “went to their tents.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT has “Adoram” here, but the Old Greek translation and Syriac Peshitta have “Adoniram.” Cf. {{1 Kings 4:6|1 Kgs 4:6}}.

*Study note:* *The work crews*. See the note on this expression in {{1 Kings 4:6|4:6}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there was no one [following] after the house of David except the tribe of Judah, it alone.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he summoned all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen men, accomplished in war.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying.”
*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek translation has here a lengthy section consisting of twenty-three verses that are not found in the MT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said in his heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Now the kingdom could return to the house of David.” The imperfect verbal form translated “could return” is understood as having a potential force here. Perhaps this is not strong enough; another option is “will return.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heart of these people could return to their master.”

*Translator's note:* The words “with his advisers” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and this thing became a sin.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “and the people went before the one to Dan.” It is likely that some words have been accidentally omitted and that the text originally said, “and the people went before the one at Bethel and before the one at Dan.”
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has the singular, but the plural is preferable here (see {{1 Kings 13:32|1 Kgs 13:32}}). The Old Greek translation and the Vulgate have the plural.

*Study note:* The *eighth month* would correspond to October-November in modern reckoning.

*Study note:* *The festival celebrated in Judah* probably refers to the Feast of Tabernacles (i.e., Booths or Temporary Shelters), held in the seventh month (September-October). See also {{1 Kings 8:2|1 Kgs 8:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he offered up [sacrifices] on the altar; he did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves which he had made.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which he had chosen by himself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Jeroboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* The Hebrew particle הִנֵּה (hinneh) is a rhetorical device by which the author invites the reader to visualize the scene for dramatic effect.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man of God.” Also in vv. {{1 Kings 13:4|4-8}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “in keeping with” (also at vv. {{1 Kings 13:2|2}}, {{1 Kings 13:5|5}}, {{1 Kings 13:9|9}}, {{1 Kings 13:17|17}}, {{1 Kings 13:18|18}}, {{1 Kings 13:32|32}}).
*Study note:* *“Look*…*you.”* For the fulfillment of this prophecy see {{2 Kings 23:15|2 Kgs 23:15-20}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fat,” i.e., fat mixed with ashes from the altar (*HALOT* 234 s.v. דשׁן).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “extended his hand from the altar.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* The verb יָבֵשׁ (yavesh) usually describes water sources as dry or plants as dry and withered. Applied to a hand or an arm (Zech 11:17), it probably means to be(come) stiff, feeble, or both. TEV and NLT interpret this as “became paralyzed.”
*Translator's note:* The fat mixed with ashes. See note v. {{1 Kings 13:3|3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “answered and said to.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “appease” or “soften the face of,” twice in this verse.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house,” representing one’s estate or possessions.

*Text-critical note:* The MT has the singular but the LXX, Syriac, some Latin manuscripts and two medieval Hebrew manuscripts have the plural, which consistent with the end of the verse and vv. {{1 Kings 13:12|12-13}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man of God.” Also in vv. {{1 Kings 13:12|12}}, {{1 Kings 13:14|14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the words which he had spoken to the king, and they told them to their father.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads וַיִּרְאוּ (vayyirʾu, “they saw”) the Qal preterite of רָאָה (raʾah, “to see”). Some translations render this as pluperfect “they had seen” (KJV, NASB), but then the verb should have been preceded by a different construction. Other translations (NIV, ESV, NRSV) follow some ancient versions and emend the verbal form to a Hiphil with pronominal suffix וַיַּרְאֻהוּ (vayyarʾuhu, “and they showed him”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am unable to return with you or to go with you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.”

*Study note:* *He had lied to him*. The motives and actions of the old prophet are difficult to understand. The old man’s response to the prophet’s death (see vv. {{1 Kings 13:26|26-32}}) suggests he did not trick him with malicious intent. Perhaps the old prophet wanted the honor of entertaining such a celebrity, or perhaps simply desired some social interaction with a fellow prophet.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man of God.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has “because” at the beginning of the sentence. In the Hebrew text vv. {{1 Kings 13:21|21-22}} are one long sentence comprised of a causal clause giving the reason for divine punishment (vv. {{1 Kings 13:21|21-22a}}) and the main clause announcing the punishment (v. {{1 Kings 13:22|22b}}). The translation divides this lengthy sentence for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mouth.”

*Translator's note:* “Therefore” is added for stylistic reasons. See the note at {{1 Kings 13:21|1 Kgs 13:21}} pertaining to the grammatical structure of vv. {{1 Kings 13:21|21-22}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will not come to the tomb of your fathers.”

*Translator's note:* The MT does not include “water” though it is implied and included in the LXX and Syriac versions.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.”
*Translator's note:* The words “what they had seen” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man of God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the mouth of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “destroyed him,” or “maimed him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the prophet.” The word “old” has been supplied in the translation to distinguish this individual from the other prophet.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man of God.”
*Translator's note:* “They” is the reading of the Hebrew text here; perhaps this is meant to include not only the old prophet but his sons (cf. v. {{1 Kings 13:31|31}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Samaria.” The name of Israel’s capital city here stands for the northern kingdom as a whole. Actually Samaria was not built and named until several years after this (see {{1 Kings 16:24|1 Kgs 16:24}}), so it is likely that the author of Kings, writing at a later time, is here adapting the old prophet’s original statement.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not turn from his evil way.”

*Study note:* The expression *common people* refers to people who were not Levites. See {{1 Kings 12:31|1 Kgs 12:31}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and one who had the desire he was filling his hand so that he became [one of] the priests of the high places.”
*Text-critical note:* Some mss of the Old Greek lack vv. {{1 Kings 14:1|1-20}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Get up, change yourself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look, Ahijah the prophet is there; he spoke about me as king over this nation.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the wife of Jeroboam did so; she arose and went to Shiloh and entered the house of Ahijah.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his eyes were set because of his old age.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like this and like this.”

*Study note:* *Tell her such and such*. Certainly the Lord gave Ahijah a specific message to give to Jeroboam’s wife (see vv. {{1 Kings 14:6|6-16}}), but the author of Kings here condenses the Lord’s message with the words “so-and-so.” For dramatic effect he prefers to have us hear the message from Ahijah’s lips as he speaks to the king’s wife.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am sent to you [with] a hard [message].”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has “because” at the beginning of the sentence. In the Hebrew text vv. {{1 Kings 14:7|7-11}} are one long sentence comprised of a causal clause giving the reason for divine punishment (vv. {{1 Kings 14:7|7-9}}) and the main clause announcing the punishment (vv. {{1 Kings 14:10|10-11}}). The translation divides this lengthy sentence for stylistic reasons.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what was right in my eyes.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you went and you made for yourself other gods, and metal [ones], angering me, and you threw me behind your back.”

*Study note:* *Disaster*. There is a wordplay in the Hebrew text. The word translated “disaster” (רָעָה, raʿah) is from the same root as the expression “you have sinned” in v. {{1 Kings 14:9|9}} (וַתָּרַע [vattaraʿ], from רָעַע, [raʿaʿ]). Jeroboam’s sins would receive an appropriate punishment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I will cut off from Jeroboam those who urinate against a wall (including both those who are) restrained and let free (or “abandoned”) in Israel.” The precise meaning of the idiomatic phrase עָצוּר וְעָזוּב (ʿatsur veʿazuv) is uncertain. For various options see *HALOT* 871 s.v. עצר 6 and M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, *II Kings* (AB), 107. The two terms are usually taken as polar opposites (“slaves and freemen” or “minors and adults”), but Cogan and Tadmor, on the basis of contextual considerations (note the usage with אֶפֶס [ʾefes], “nothing but”) in {{Deuteronomy 32:36|Deut 32:36}} and {{2 Kings 14:26|2 Kgs 14:26}}, argue convincingly that the terms are synonyms, meaning “restrained and abandoned,” and refer to incapable or incapacitated individuals.

*Translator's note:* The traditional view understands the verb בָּעַר (baʿar) to mean “burn.” Manure was sometimes used as fuel (see {{Ezekiel 4:12|Ezek 4:12}}, {{Ezekiel 4:15|15}}). However, an alternate view takes בָּעַר as a homonym meaning “sweep away” (*HALOT* 146 s.v. II בער). In this case one might translate, “I will sweep away the dynasty of Jeroboam, just as one sweeps away manure it is gone” (cf. ASV, NASB, TEV). Either metaphor emphasizes the thorough and destructive nature of the coming judgment.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has “belonging to Jeroboam” here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “This is the day. What also now?” The precise meaning of the second half of the statement is uncertain.

*Translator's note:* The elliptical Hebrew text reads literally “and the Lord will strike Israel as a reed sways in the water.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fathers” (also in vv. {{1 Kings 14:22|22}}, {{1 Kings 14:31|31}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the River.” In biblical Hebrew this is a typical reference to the Euphrates River. The name “Euphrates” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* *Asherah* was a leading deity of the Canaanite pantheon, wife/sister of El and goddess of fertility. She was commonly worshiped at shrines in or near groves of evergreen trees, or, failing that, at places marked by wooden poles. These were to be burned or cut down ({{Deuteronomy 12:3|Deut 12:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:21|16:21}}; {{Judges 6:25|Judg 6:25}}, {{Judges 6:28|28}}, {{Judges 6:30|30}}; {{2 Kings 18:4|2 Kgs 18:4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because they made their Asherah poles that anger the Lord”; or “their images of Asherah”; ASV, NASB “their Asherim”; NCV “they set up idols to worship Asherah.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the events of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he ruled, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Rehoboam.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the city where the Lord chose to place his name from all the tribes of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “an Ammonite”; the word “woman” is implied by the gender of the word.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they made him jealous more than all which their fathers had done by their sins which they sinned.”

*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek translation has “a conspiracy” rather than “male cultic prostitutes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they did according to all the abominable acts of the nations.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the events of Rehoboam, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down with his fathers.”

*Translator's note:* In the Hebrew text the name is spelled “Abijam” here and in {{1 Kings 15:1|1 Kgs 15:1-8}}.
*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek also has the phrase “the son of Rehoboam.”
*Study note:* *Abishalom* (also in v. {{1 Kings 15:10|10}}) is a variant of the name Absalom (cf. 2 Chr 11:20). The more common form is used by TEV, NLT.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his heart was not complete with the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “gave him a lamp.”

*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek has the plural “his sons.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by raising up his son after him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and by causing Jerusalem to stand firm.”

*Translator's note:* The words “he did this” are added for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what was right in the eyes of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and had not turned aside from all which he commanded him.”

*Text-critical note:* Most Hebrew mss read “Rehoboam”; a few Hebrew mss and the Syriac read “Abijam” (a variant of Abijah).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (Abijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the events of Abijah, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down with his fathers.” The Old Greek also has these words: “in the twenty-eighth year of Jeroboam.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they buried him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mother,” but Hebrew often uses the terms “father” and “mother” for grandparents and more remote ancestors.

*Study note:* This episode is especially significant in light of Ahab’s decision to promote Baal worship in Israel. In Canaanite mythology the drought that swept over the region (v. {{1 Kings 17:1|1}}) would signal that Baal, a fertility god responsible for providing food for his subjects, had been defeated by the god of death and was imprisoned in the underworld. While Baal was overcome by death and unable to function like a king, Israel’s God demonstrated his sovereignty and superiority to death by providing food for a widow and restoring life to her son. And he did it all in Sidonian territory, Baal’s back yard, as it were. The episode demonstrates that Israel’s God, not Baal, is the true king who provides food and controls life and death. This polemic against Baalism reaches its climax in the next chapter, when the Lord proves that he, not Baal, controls the elements of the storm and determines when the rains will fall.
